p:cNvPr.descr: Three illustrations of cell membranes showing the different manners in which they can curve or flatten by way of protein activity. (a) The top model is an illustration of a curved section of a cell membrane. The membrane has the standard blue heads on the inside and outside of the membrane with the yellow tails in the center. The top of the membrane is interspersed with small red dots, each of which has a + sign above it. The plus signs are encompassed by a large pale blue region, which mirrors the curve of the membrane. A gray text box below reads, “A protein with intrinsic curvature and with a high density of positive charge on its concave surface interacts with negatively charged phospholipid head groups, favoring curvature of the bilayer.” (b) Below, the membrane now has two small black helices embedded sideways into the membrane on both ends, forcing the membrane to bend sharply downward to the left and right. The blue and yellow lipid units on the ends of the membrane segment are crowded together as a result. The red heads with + signs above them are still present at the top of the membrane, and the pale blue curve above is sharper than previously described. A gray text box below reads, “A protein with one or several amphipathic helices inserted into one leaflet of the bilayer crowds the lipids in that leaflet, forcing the membrane to bend.” (c) Finally, the membrane without the red heads or + signs. Instead, the curved membrane has a mass of blue helical proteins bonded to the top. The mass bonds to two points on the membrane and leaves a gap in the center between the proteins and the membrane. A gray text box below reads, “Proteins with BAR domains can polymerize into a superstructure that favors and maintains the curvature.”
